item.title: Induction
item.description:
Induction is a method of finding regularities and formulating empirical laws based on observations. It's focus on causal relations makes it typical of the Nomothetic Approach. A researcher practicing induction will observe a common feature in a few cases. This might look as follows: Case 1 has property A and property B Case 2 has property A and property B and so on As more cases of this are observed you could make an inductive generalization that when property A is present in a case so is property B. Swan Example (from lecture) Case 1 is a swan with white feathers Case 2 is a swan with white feathers and so on Inductive generalization: all swans are white Induction is ampliative, meaning inductive inference makes claims that are beyond the scope of what has been observed. That is why inductive reasoning is often criticized, it uses a small sample and assumes all cases are like this. But if you were to find only a single black swan you would immediately make the generalization from above false. The course highlights that induction is a useful tool of inquiry so long as you account for these risks.
For more on these criticisms read Hume's Problem of Induction
Lecture 3 slides 19-23

item.title: Correspondence Theory of Truth
item.description:
Truth is a property, a binary property of beliefs. So you can say either "yes, that belief is true" or "no, that belief is not true" (aka it is false). This is what we mean by binary, it is either one or the other. If you are familiar with computer science, truth is a boolean.The correspondence theory of truth says that a proposition is true if and only if there is a fact corresponding to it. Frustratingly this only leads to the question of "Wtf is a fact then?". Truth and fact are very similar (I am sure you use them interchangeably in every day speech). But for Philosophy of Science we make a distinction. Truth, as mentioned at the start, is a property of a person's belief. What is believed is either true or false. But a fact is objective. A fact is a state of affairs. A fact is a property of the world (or universe). Facts exist even if there were no humans around to make propositions (or to have beliefs). Facts make propositions true. A fact is neither true nor false. A fact either is a fact or it is not. Truth and falsity are properties of propositions which individuals make.Bertrand Russell, The Problems of Philosophy (1912) Thus a belief is true when there is a corresponding fact, and is false when there is no corresponding fact... What makes a belief true is a fact, and this fact does not (except in exceptional cases) in any way involve the mind of the person who has the belief.
This quote is in Lecture 2 slide 22 but I cut out some confusing and unnecessary fluff from the middle\Quick Test Question: an astronomer observing space could correctly conclude "Mars is red". What is the corresponding fact to this truth? The astronomer's careful observation and scientific expertise The consensus among astronomers that Mars appears red Mars itself. The fact that Mars is actually red in reality All previous observations of mars have determined it is red Click here for the answer Mars itself. The fact that Mars is actually red in reality Explanation Facts are parts of reality, they have nothing to do with human interpretation, observation, etc. It can not be option 1 because it is based on observation. it cannot be option 2 because it is based on common belief of astronomers. And for both reasons it cannot be option 4. This leaves us option 3 which is based on the intrinsic and objective features of Mars. If facts are aspects of reality, how do we determine truth for more abstract concepts? If truth is dependent on the existence of a corresponding fact can we say "7 is a prime number" is true? Where does that fact originate? Or how about saying "murder is wrong", in an overwhelming number of societies this is agreed upon, but is it possible to say that this is true? This is the criticism of the theory.The criticism put simply Correspondence theory of truth is not sufficient for more abstract ideas.
Lecture 2 Workgroup 2

item.title: Hume's Problem of Induction
item.description:
David Hume was a historian and philosopher of the Scottish Enlightenment. He wrote on the issues of inductive reasoning. He found that neither Induction, which over generalized, nor deduction, which had too narrow a scope, were ideal. He concluded that inductive generalizations had no logical foundations. He argued further that ampliative generalizations like induction are "psychological tendencies of the human mind".
So what is to be done? Despite the way Karl R. Popper later ran with Hume's problem of induction, Hume himself did not call for an outright abandonment of practicing induction. The "pragmatic warrant" argument has arose to say that despite its imperfections, induction is a practical means to formulate hypothesis.
Lecture 3 slides 23-26

item.title: Justified True Belief (JTB) Account of Knowledge
item.description:
The Justified True Belief (JTB) Account of Knowledge offers one explanation for the question "What is Knowledge?". The JTB account is specifically concerned with explaining Propositional Knowledge. As the name suggests, it defines (propositional) knowledge as a justified true belief. This account of knowledge was first proposed by Plato.A knows that P if and only if
P is true A believes that P A is justified in believing that P A is a person, P is a proposition Take the below statement. "Adam knows that there is a door over there" This statement is made up of two parts that we are concerned ofWe have the person Adam (A) "Adam knows that there is a door behind him" Then we have "there is a door over there" this is our proposition (P). "Adam knows that there is a door behind him"
For more on what differentiates propositional knowledge from other knowledge see Propositional Knowledge.
Elaborating on Lecture 2 page 9 Adam has the knowledge that there is a door behind him if and only if: There is a door behind Adam (P is true) Adam believes there is a door behind him (A believes that P) Adam is justified in believing that there is a door behind him (A is justified in believing that P)
Only with all 3 of these condition does Adam know there is a door behind him. If any number of these conditions are missing then it is not Knowledge.
The first condition is that the proposition must be true. In our example this would mean there must actually be a door behind Adam. As long as there is a door behind Adam you can continue through the conditions. Whether or not Adam is aware of the door behind him is not important for this condition.You can't know something if it is not true.The second condition is that the person believes the proposition. In our example this would mean that Adam needs to believe there is a door behind him. You can't know something if you do not believe it.The final condition is that the person is justified in believing the proposition. In our example this would mean that Adam needs to have a fair reason to believe there is a door behind him. But what do we mean by justified? James writes that to be justified is "to have good grounds for holding a belief". There must be a rational thought process or experience which led to your belief. If Adam had seen the door just before turning around, he would be justified in believing that there is a door behind him. He would not be justified to believe that in the 2 seconds he turned around someone had removed the door off of it's hinges and carried it away. That would be an unjustified belief.
This final condition is there to ensure someone guessing is not considered knowledge. If Adam woke up blindfolded in a room and simply guessed that there was a door behind him, even if that was true, you would not say that Adam knows there is a door behind him. If you have no reason for believing something, you do not know that.
Pulled from Lecture 2 slide 17 but it is really good for getting the idea.

Lecture 2 - slides 8-18

item.title: Knowledge
item.description:
For Philosophy of Science we are mainly focused on the Justified True Belief (JTB) Account of Knowledge."I know The Hague". This type of knowledge is less concrete and defined, it is not necessarily bound. Another way to word it would be familiarity. "I am familiar with The Hague". (If you know French this would be connaître, not savoir)"I know how to ride a bike". This type of knowledge refers to ability. You could say "I am able to ride a bike" and communicate the same fact.Propositional knowledge is what this course is predominantly concerned with. The slides break it down into 4 sub categories"I know that there is a door over there". This is knowledge of the world and how things are.
"I know that the sun will rise tomorrow". This one is weird and confusing even for me. But from speaking to James about it I get the idea that this is considered knowledge by the JTB Account because you are justified in believing that the sun will rise tomorrow. (If someone started shouting that the sun is about to explode you'd probably call them crazy). That being said I don't know how this meets the first condition. How can something that has not yet happened be true?
If you have an explanation find my contact info on the main page."I know that 7 + 5 = 12". Not much more too it. I suck at math won't try to say more than needed.
Lecture 2 - sheets 5-7

item.title: Social Sciences
item.description:
The social sciences are the youngest of the 3 disciplines (Social Sciences, Human Sciences, and Natural Sciences). They originated in the late 1800s, particularly in French and German academics, where early scholars of the social sciences like Comte, Durkheim, and Weber began exploring how to study societies. Sociology Political Science Economics Psychology Anthropology Demography (the study of demographics)
Social Science sits between the natural and human science. Fields like economics and demography tend to take nomothetic approaches, often utilizing math to investigate society and identify underlying structures. On the other hand, fields like cultural anthropology, sociology, and political science utilize idiographic approaches through which they aim to understand, interpret, and ascribe meaning to societal phenomena and behavior.
But that is not to say any field falls entirely within a single approach. Psychology for example uses both. The sub-field of Psychometrics aims to measure, categorize, and quantify psychological observations and tests. This is a distinctly nomothetic method. But as was detailed in the idiographic note's section on Freud and Little Hans, Psychology can also be very idiographic in its methodology.

item.title: Natural Sciences
item.description:
The natural sciences are ancient, but the landscape of the discipline we know today was shaped in part during the middle ages in China, India, and the Islamic world, and later Europe during the Renaissance. Physics Chemistry Biology Astronomy The natural sciences operate on the premise that the physical universe is uniform and simple. It is for that reason that they are concerned with universals and regularities, by extension this is why they are dominated by the Nomothetic Approach. Example: dropping a stone If you drop a stone, the natural sciences do not care about you as the individual dropping the stone, what motivated you to do so, how the stone ended up in your hands, etc. Instead they are concerned with the underlying natural law(s) which made the stone fall (gravity).
As overwhelmingly nomothetic fields, the natural sciences seek to formulate or "discover" laws of nature (see elaborations here). These laws are held by some, even outside the natural sciences, to be the highest form of scientific knowledge. The laws of gravity, thermodynamics, etc. all fall under the "laws of nature". Some complications The groups of disciplines are more diverse and complicated than may be described. The picture given is of course a simplification. While natural sciences do generally value laws, this is less valuable in biology, cell biology for example where mechanisms take priority. In the human sciences, fields such as linguistics and archaeology use some methods inspired by the natural sciences. Marxist historiography for example go against the human sciences distrust of generalization, believing in universal laws of historical development.

item.title: Human Sciences
item.description:
The human sciences are quite old endeavors. The fields of grammar, logic, and rhetoric were studied in the middle ages at the University of Bologna. But they were seen as techniques and instructions more so than a field of study. This shifted during the Renaissance of humanism in the 16th century. That process formalized the human sciences and continued through to the 19th century. History Art History Linguistics Literary Studies Philosophy Religious Studies The world studied by the human sciences is made up of historical human actors. These actors are creative, from them originates acts, texts, works of art. This creation does not follow rules but instead is conceptualized as unpredictable and inexplicable. Acts Example: Caesar crossing the Rubicon Caesar crossing the Rubicon was an act. The act originated from him. The same can be said for the creation of a work of art. The human sciences zoom in on historical particularity (much the inverse of the Natural Sciences). Each event and its context is regarded as wholly unique. The human sciences identify eras such as the renaissance or enlightenment, but these act only as taxonomical categories for subjects of study to be placed into, they are not accompanied by any general rule for that period.
The human sciences have an intrinsic distrust for generalizations or idealizations. The highest for of knowledge in these fields is intimate knowledge of the particular: the life and acts of a certain figure, or even acts at a particular time. There is little to no use for the prospect of scientific laws and as such the human sciences are especially oriented around the Idiographic Approach.
If laws of nature are the most impressive format and the core output of the Natural Sciences then the human sciences' core output is interpretations. Interpretations of acts, texts, and artworks are often embedded in theoretical frameworks through which there is an attempt to reconstruct the historical actor's world of experience and meanings. These interpretations can then be tested against the text or other material of that actor. When generated thoroughly the interpretation can be considered quite objective. Some complications The groups of disciplines are more diverse and complicated than may be described. The picture given is of course a simplification. While natural sciences do generally value laws, this is less valuable in biology, cell biology for example where mechanisms take priority. In the human sciences, fields such as linguistics and archaeology use some methods inspired by the natural sciences. Marxist historiography for example go against the human sciences distrust of generalization, believing in universal laws of historical development.

item.title: Idiographic Approach
item.description:
Philosophy of Science introduces two approaches for describing the world: Nomothetic and Idiographic. These two approaches help us to conceptualize the difference between Natural Sciencesand Human Sciences as well as analyze the diversity of the Social Sciences. These approaches are possibly the two most important concepts for the course as they are routinely connected to other concepts.
See Lecture 1 for more
The Idiographic approach concerns itself with understanding. This is a key factor which differentiates it from the Nomothetic Approach, which aims to explain. The idiographic approach is typical of the Human Sciences.The strength of the idiographic approach is in identifying differences between cases which might otherwise appear similar. It brings to light the details and context-specific knowledge for an object of study.The weakness of the idiographic approach is that it may not account for laws, structures, or constraints which influence an outcome. Furthermore, because it focuses on a single case, findings can not be generalized. In this way it may believe an observation to be unique when it is in fact common.
Sigmund Freud studied a 5 year old's fear of horses in 1909. In doing so he accumulated ~150 pages of clinical notes in which he delved into extraordinary detail about a single child's psychology. Freud did not aim to use this study to state "all children who are scared of horses behave like Little Hans". He did not want to formulate a law or a theory like a Nomothetic Approach would result in. His approach was solely interested in Little Hans, his case, his life, his fear. In doing so he was able to deeply understand a specific instance of horse phobia. The below elaboration is not based in the reality of Freud's study and is for illustrative purposes The strength of a study like this is that Freud may have been able to offer the boy or his parents advice for tackling the fear that only a deep understanding of the boy's mind could give. Perhaps he identified a unique cause of the fear which could be specifically addressed.But on the other hand, Freud may not have considered more general solutions. Exposure therapy, or "facing your fears", is common advice for overcoming them. Being so focused on the unique characteristics of Little Hans' fear, Freud may not have suggested such a widely applicable solution. That being said, if exposure therapy and other common solutions did not work, an idiographic approach becomes very important as the only way to discover a solution.
Lecture 1

item.title: Nomothetic Approach
item.description:
Philosophy of Science introduces two approaches for describing the world: Nomothetic and Idiographic. These two approaches help us to conceptualize the difference between Natural Sciencesand Human Sciences as well as analyze the diversity of the Social Sciences. These approaches are possibly the two most important concepts for the course as they are routinely connected to other concepts
See Lecture 1 for more
The nomothetic approach aims to explain. Explanation is a term you will find in the nomothetic approach, far less so in the Idiographic Approach.Im not reading all that Nomothetic gives you "laws". Think of the laws of gravity or thermodynamics. Those are derived from this approach. The nomothetic approach concerns itself with: Identifying regularities in the world Formulating generalizations and laws to describe those regularities Deriving explanations of observed outcomes based on these generalizations and laws. The above is copied almost exactly from the slides but it is how he words it in more than one lecture.
The nomothetic approach is typical practice for the natural sciences. That being said it does find uses in the human and social sciences.The nomothetic approach is useful for finding similarities and structures which underlie subjects of study which can seem diverse on the surface. The product of the nomothetic approach is broad "general" knowledgeThe nomothetic approach fails to represent the uniqueness of a given case. In this way it can be said to simplify complex ideas (which in some contexts also serves as a strength). Critics of the method argue it is reductive.
See Lecture 3 for more
Physics has identified "laws of nature". These laws identify certain characteristics of the universes function. In the Natural Sciences (like physics), laws are mathematical equations. These laws are universal. This means they do not only apply only in certain cases, but in every case across the universe. This is often the case in the natural sciences. James provides two examples in his slides, and I will offer an additional one. Do not get bogged down in these examples if they are confusing for you. I have done my best to explain them without getting into the details of the equations but I am not certain I have done a great job at that. Suggestions for making this more understandable are welcomed.If the equation above makes no sense to you don't worry it is not important and just might help those who do understand it. The important thing is that you understand this equation is used to determine the gravitational force (F) between two masses (m1 & m2). This equation might be used to determine the gravitational force between the sun and the earth. Without knowing this law we would not know that the gravity effecting objects can be reliably calculated. These are the type of laws the natural sciences are concerned with.
Again don't stress the equation if it is not your cup of tea. Understand though that it is used to reliably determine how quickly an element decays (little pieces breaking off) over time (t) based on a known constant (the rate of decay, represented by λ). This equation, as with the previous, represents functions of the universe, hence the term "universal" to say they apply in every case (as far as we have observed, more on that caveat in Falsificationism).If the examples from the slides didn't quite click I will offer my own example. You might be familiar with Einstein's mass–energy equivalence, it is fairly iconic and simple. A brief (massively oversimplified) explanation is that the energy of a particle (E) is equivalent to the mass of that particle (m), multiplied by the speed of light squared (c2). A practical use for this in terms you may understand is nuclear weapons. In a nuclear weapon there is a mass of an element. If we wanted to determine the energy released in that explosion we would be able to calculate that using this law of mass-energy equivalence because nuclear bombs function by turning the mass to energy. From these examples you should take away that these laws of nature are used for not only explaining how the universe works, but also for achieving practical effects. This is what is meant by "applying" a law.
See Lecture 3 for more
The nomothetic approach is also used in the Social Sciences as well as Human Sciences. Laws in these sciences are slightly different from the laws of nature. They are not typically represented by equations but that is not to say they are never represented by equations (remember the GPE midterm for example). The nomothetic approach in these sciences assume that "human affairs exhibit significant regularities".
Here I will use just two examples, both from the slides. He offers 4 in the slides so if these are no good for you start from page 9 in Lecture 3. I will start with a simple one before moving on to a complex one, after which I'll offer a critical approach which will answer the obvious questions that arise.Democratic peace theory argues that democratic states do not fight wars against one another. This is not quantifiable into a formula like we saw with physics. Instead it is a more nuanced relationship which is dependent on the definition of democracy and war.I will preface by saying skip this example if you have zero interest in economics and/or physics because it might be too much and not necessary. That being said it may be interesting for some to see a case where a social science turns a law into a formula.
There is a subsection of economics which attempts to take the physical laws of nature and morph them into economic laws. I'll ask you to recall The Inverse-Square law from above. Economics took that same structure and applied it to international trade:In this equation V is the volume of trade between two countries (It replaces F from the inverse-square law) m1 and m2 are the economic sizes of those countries (just as they represent object mass in physics), d is the geographical distance between those countries, G serves as a proportionality constant. This similarity has been used to suggest a certain relationship between physics and economics. Put simply, this equation represents the fact that trade volume decreases as distance between trading partners grow. This relationship has in fact been observed in the real world. Where it differs however is it's predictive ability. Unlike the natural sciences there is no way to calculate any of these variables precisely. If you know all of the real-world numbers to fill in for the variables on the right side of the equation, V would not perfectly match what is observed like it would be with determining F in the inverse-square law.Despite its lack of precise accuracy, the value in putting this into a mathematic equation is how it allows us to model economics. If you wanted to know whether to trade with a larger country that is farther from you or a smaller country that is closer to you, you can roughly make a prediction using this formula for which option would be more beneficial. Such considerations are absent from the Heckscher–Ohlin model of trade which is concerned only with production efficiency, not the efficiency of transport from producer to consumer.You might be saying "but democratic states have fought one another". This problem arises because of that dependence on the definition of democracy and war that I mentioned. In 1969 El Salvador and Honduras fought a war against one another. Both states had held elections, but in practice the military held most of the power. Those looking to defend the theory argue simply that these states are not democracies. Whilst that may be a valid argument it brings to light the criticisms directed towards the use of the nomothetic approach in the human and social sciences: they are too complex and nuanced to be simplified into laws. These laws are based on the assumption that human affairs, no matter the cultural or situational factors, have certain patterns and regularities which emerge.The Takeaway You should take away from this the fact that there is a discourse amongst scholars over the use of this approach in these fields. There is no "right" answer on whether or not they should be used. You might notice for example that it is labeled "Democratic Peace Theory" and not "The Democratic Peace Law". This embodies the difference quite well. Democratic Peace Law sounds far less disputable than a theory.
